Potassium. A soft, reactive alkali metal with atomic number nineteen, symbol K, and an essential macronutrient for all living organisms. Organisms maintain high intracellular potassium and low extracellular potassium via active transport. This electrochemical gradient drives nerve impulses, muscle contraction, and osmotic regulation, making potassium fundamental to animal and plant physiology.

Potassium is the eighth most abundant element in the Earth's crust and is highly soluble in water as a monovalent cation. The sodium-potassium pump, the Na-plus/K-plus ATPase, actively transports three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, consuming ATP. This gradient is the electrochemical basis of all excitable cells.

Resting membrane potential in neurons around minus seventy millivolts arises from the potassium gradient and the relative permeability of potassium and sodium channels. Action potentials depend critically on potassium efflux repolarizing the membrane. In skeletal muscle, potassium release during contraction can raise extracellular potassium transiently. Severe hyperkalaemia—excess potassium—can cause cardiac arrhythmias or cardiac arrest.

Potassium is an essential macronutrient for plants. It controls stomatal opening via guard cell turgor, maintains cell osmotic potential, and activates numerous enzymes in photosynthesis and carbohydrate metabolism. Dietary potassium from fruit, vegetables, and nuts is critical in humans. Deficiency, or hypokalaemia, causes muscle weakness, arrhythmias, and impaired glucose metabolism. Potassium has a single stable isotope, though potassium-forty is radioactive and contributes slightly to natural background radiation in the human body.
